content: Hematologic toxicities associated with the use of Retrovir (zidovudine) appear to be influenced by the patient’s pretreatment bone marrow reserve, as well as the dose and duration of therapy. In patients with advanced symptomatic HIV-1 disease, anemia and neutropenia have been identified as the most significant adverse events. For those who develop hematologic toxicity, a reduction in hemoglobin levels may occur as early as 2 to 4 weeks into treatment, while neutropenia typically manifests after 6 to 8 weeks. There have also been reports of pancytopenia associated with Retrovir use, which in most cases was reversible upon discontinuation of the drug. However, significant anemia has been observed during treatment with Retrovir, either as monotherapy or in combination with other antiretrovirals. This anemia often necessitates dose adjustments, discontinuation of Retrovir, and/or blood transfusions. Frequent blood count monitoring is strongly recommended, particularly in patients with poor bone marrow reserve or advanced HIV-1 disease, to detect severe anemia or neutropenia early. For individuals with asymptomatic or early HIV-1 disease, periodic blood counts are advised. If anemia or neutropenia develops, dosage interruption may be required. Myopathy and myositis, characterized by pathological changes similar to those caused by HIV-1 disease itself, have been associated with prolonged use of Retrovir. Lactic acidosis and severe hepatomegaly with steatosis, including fatal cases, have been reported with the use of nucleoside analogues, such as zidovudine, either alone or in combination with other antiretrovirals. These events have been more commonly observed in women, and risk factors may include obesity and prolonged exposure to antiretroviral nucleoside analogues. Caution is advised when administering Retrovir to patients with known risk factors for liver disease, although cases have also been reported in patients without any known risk factors. Treatment with Retrovir should be discontinued in any patient who develops clinical or laboratory findings suggestive of lactic acidosis or significant hepatotoxicity, which may include hepatomegaly and steatosis, even in the absence of marked transaminase elevations. In HIV-1/HCV co-infected patients, in vitro studies have shown that ribavirin can reduce the phosphorylation of pyrimidine nucleoside analogues, such as zidovudine. Co-administration of ribavirin and zidovudine has been associated with exacerbation of anemia and a loss of virologic suppression for HIV-1/HCV. Therefore, co-administration of ribavirin and zidovudine is not recommended. Consideration should be given to replacing zidovudine in established combination HIV-1/HCV therapy, particularly in patients with a history of zidovudine-induced anemia. Hepatic decompensation, including fatal cases, has been reported in HIV-1/HCV co-infected patients receiving combination antiretroviral therapy for HIV-1 and interferon alfa with or without ribavirin. Patients receiving these therapies should be closely monitored for treatment-associated toxicities, including hepatic decompensation, neutropenia, and anemia. Discontinuation of zidovudine should be considered when medically appropriate. Immune reconstitution syndrome has been reported in patients treated with combination antiretroviral therapy, including Retrovir. During the initial phase of treatment, patients with improving immune systems may develop an inflammatory response to indolent or residual opportunistic infections, such as Mycobacterium avium infection, cytomegalovirus, Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, or tuberculosis. This may require further evaluation and treatment. Autoimmune disorders, such as Graves’ disease, polymyositis, and Guillain-Barré syndrome, have also been reported in the context of immune reconstitution. However, the onset of these conditions is more variable and can occur many months after initiating treatment. Redistribution or accumulation of body fat, including central obesity, dorsocervical fat enlargement (buffalo hump), peripheral wasting, facial wasting, breast enlargement, and a Cushingoid appearance, has been observed in patients receiving antiretroviral therapy. The mechanism and long-term consequences of these events are currently unknown, and a causal relationship has not been established.
